clue.text: Commercial yarn bags prone to losing colour

indicators.note: to bag something is to capture it and hold it inside, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: a yarn is a tall story, a fable
a commercial is a TV advertisement, an ad

explanation.surface: Cheap advertised wool that fades badly in the wash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' looks like wool to match 'losing colour', but here it is a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fadable is able to fade, so its dye washes out or bleaches over time.

clue.text: I would never fib, former mate is wrong

indicators.note: if the letters are wrong as they stand, they must be put right by rearranging them

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone protests that they never lie, and their ex is mistaken.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a polite disclaimer saying the speaker would never presume or dare to do something.

clue.text: Bird conveyed upwards protecting soft strip of feathers

to protect something is to surround and shield it, so a letter sits inside

to lead is to convey or guide
p is piano, the musical marking for soft

explanation.walkthrough: 'Conveyed' looks like a definition but it is a word to be joined to the bird before the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: To deplume is the dictionary verb for plucking a bird, removing its plumage.

clue.text: Chap fine participating in ballet regularly

to participate in something is to be part of it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters

explanation.definitionFit: Bloke is informal British slang for a man, the same as chap or guy.

clue.text: Drew out extremely immoral rogue with deceit

blocks.note: its first and last letters
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rogue' reads as a noun in the surface but works as an adjective meaning disordered.
explanation.definitionFit: To elicit is to draw out a response or information from someone.

clue.text: Long sections of wood somewhere in the West Midlands

blocks.note: first meaning: poles or rods, plural
second meaning: the abbreviation for Staffordshire, an English county

explanation.surface: Timber planks found in a region of central England.
explanation.walkthrough: Staffs is the standard abbreviation for Staffordshire, a county in the English West Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffs are long sticks or poles, and Staffs is also the short name for an English county.

clue.text: Exclusive group infiltrated by the Parisian

clue.text: They affirm cheers upset barking setters

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read from bottom to top
barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go crazy

blocks.note: ta is British slang for thanks
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking setters' paints noisy dogs, but barking means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Attesters bear witness, declaring that something is true or genuine.

clue.text: Confusion with scrap taking place in Portuguese city

clue.text: Bird of prey’s activated trap by den over to the west

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, meaning of birds of prey

in an across clue, west is leftwards, so the letters run right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
a lair is an animal's den
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A hawk set off a trap next to its den.
explanation.definitionFit: Raptorial is the adjective for raptors, birds of prey that seize with talons.

clue.text: Fatigued in rows, expending energy

explanation.walkthrough: One E is dropped from TIERED.

clue.text: Business releases rent for airport shop, perhaps

clue.text: Turning nibbed utensil penning musical composition

turning round means the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nibbed utensil' looks like a cryptic pen, but its letters hold the answer backwards.

clue.text: Relentless princess antagonised hosts

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

clue.text: Person attempting to embrace tip to be less boomerish

explanation.walkthrough: A boomer, slang for an older person from the post-war baby boom, is the stereotype of being out of touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Being trendier means more fashionable and current, the opposite of an old-fashioned boomer.

clue.text: Pack mitts for sailors

mitts is slang for hands

explanation.surface: Packing gloves for a crew going to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pack' reads as a verb, but it is a pack of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Deckhands are ordinary crew members who work on a ship's deck.

clue.text: Start journey from outskirts of Stowe with posh type

blocks.note: its first and last letters

explanation.definitionFit: To set off is the everyday phrasal verb for beginning a trip or departing.

clue.text: Second sibling in post showing potential

S is the abbreviation for second
sib is short for sibling

clue.text: Hero ignoring that male clown, extravagant in style

blocks.note: taken as written
he is the pronoun for that male

explanation.walkthrough: HE is removed from HERO, leaving RO.

clue.text: One drawing under case in cold storage unit

one who tows, drawing something along behind

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case in cold' looks like a box in a freezer, but it is the outer letters of cold.
explanation.definitionFit: A CD tower is a tall rack for holding compact discs, a piece of storage furniture.

clue.text: Prisoners love Madame’s soup

Mme is the abbreviation for Madame

clue.text: Great feeling suitable effects after exercise class

blocks.note: PE is physical education, the school exercise lesson
aching is the fitting consequence of a workout

explanation.walkthrough: 'Great feeling' reads as one phrase, but only 'Great' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Peachy is informal for excellent or fine, as in everything is peachy.

clue.text: Unbeatable team no-one will play is such

clue.text: Daughter in eateries on vacation does this

taken as written
its first and last letters
